title: Hallucination and the Limits of Next-Token Prediction
summary: A model trained to predict likely text will produce fluent, confident text whether or not it is true. This lesson explains hallucination in terms of next-token probabilities, measures calibration, and shows how grounding, abstention and tools work around the limits of a fixed, frozen model.
objectives: Explain hallucination as the consequence of sampling plausible tokens, and why fluency is not evidence of truth
Measure calibration with a reliability table and expected calibration error
Explain how grounding in retrieved sources and abstention thresholds reduce unsupported answers
Reason about knowledge cutoffs and why a model's parameters cannot know recent or private facts
Identify tasks where fixed per-token computation and tokenization make models unreliable, and the standard workarounds
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with softmax, temperature, log-probs and entropy from [Next-Token Prediction and Sampling](/learn/model-foundations/sampling), and with how a context window works from [Context Windows, Prefill and the KV Cache](/learn/model-foundations/context-and-kv-cache). Tokenization artefacts are covered in [Tokenization](/learn/model-foundations/tokenization).
